sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] T4 'You reduce devotion to manipulation' answers T3 directly. [s2] Turn 3: 'You are both focusing on the rose's traits.' [s3] Turn 4 rebuts the Classicist's hierarchy directly; turn 5 builds on it.
sub.limitation: [s1] Existential Realist turns 5, 11 restate his own line rather than answer. [s2] Turns 7-8 turn to the user instead of answering turn 6. [s3] Turns 1-2 are parallel openings; Sartre mostly echoes Fromm.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] T4 adds love beginning as will, then maturing; T10 adds asymmetrical care. [s2] Turn 4 adds that physical presence turns an observer into a participant. [s3] Turn 8 moves from rose-as-project to rose as a mirror of his freedom.
sub.limitation: [s1] Realist repeats 'he invented/created meaning' in T2, T5, T8, T11 without new distinctions. [s2] The later turns drift to speculation about the user, not the text. [s3] Turn 8's pivot is unprompted; no objection forced it.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Inherent worth vs. value made by care; devotion vs. control (T6). [s2] Turns 2 and 5 ask whether the bond is healthy or simply a duty. [s3] Is value created by care or discovered (turns 2, 6, 9)?
sub.limitation: [s1] Rose's vanity and Prince's own regret about judging her never examined. [s2] The rose's own change (her apology, her confession) is never weighed. [s3] Leaves out the fox's lesson and the garden of five thousand roses.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] T7 Idealist absorbs critique: accept the other 'flaws and all'. [s2] Turn 6 concedes the suffering point, then reframes it as authorship. [s3] Turn 7 concedes the prince learns through the rose, then reframes that.
sub.limitation: [s1] Social Critic never adjusts; positions stay mostly parallel. [s2] The Attachment Theorist never takes in the other views. [s3] Sartre and Fromm merge ('Exactly', turn 5), so only Plato dissents.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] T12 sharpens it to partnership vs. projection. [s2] Turn 9 sharpens the question: who she is, or who he decides to be. [s3] Turn 9: is the rose a tool for self-actualization, or a window?
sub.limitation: [s1] Ending drifts from reading the book to the user's relationship preferences. [s2] It ends on the user's attachments rather than the reading. [s3] The user's 'why' about the book itself never gets a clearer answer.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] T10 fairly names the Critic's assumption that equality sets the standard. [s2] Turn 3 states both rival views fairly before redirecting. [s3] Turn 6 gives Plato's ladder a fair hearing as a necessary discipline.
sub.limitation: [s1] T3 calls the Realist's view a 'vanity project', a strawman. [s2] Turn 5's 'toxic bond' strawmans the taming view in turn 4. [s3] Turn 5 caricatures Plato as escaping the anguish of choice.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] T6 tests whether he valued his fantasy over her agency. [s2] Turn 2: 'That logic assumes all investment is healthy.' [s3] Turn 9 tests the constructivist view: is the rose merely a tool?
sub.limitation: [s1] Challenges stay abstract; no scene from the book tests them. [s2] It ignores the Prince's regret at judging her by words, not deeds. [s3] No one tests either reading against what actually happens in the book.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] Real sources; chapter 21 (fox) is the right basis for T1. [s2] Turns 1 and 4 rest on the novel itself (Chapter 21, taming). [s3] Turn 3 paraphrases Symposium 210e, Jowett's 'instructed thus far in the things of love'.
sub.limitation: [s1] T5 'live authentically' is not Camus's term; field of roses never cited. [s2] Turn 2's 'does not reciprocate' overstates it; the rose confesses her love when he leaves. [s3] Turn 3 says 'As it is written' but invents its second clause.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] T11 'We still do not know if the rose would have flourished'. [s2] Turn 8 hedges: 'It is possible the user is struggling'. [s3] 'I would argue' (turn 2) and 'One might say' (turn 3) mark interpretation.
sub.limitation: [s1] T9 guesses at the user's motive without flagging it as speculation. [s2] Turn 5 calls the bond 'toxic' as if it were fact. [s3] Turn 2 says 'literally inventing', which overstates.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: [s1] T8 'I must concede that this evolution shows a commitment'. [s2] Turn 6: 'I concede that suffering without purpose is merely trauma.' [s3] Turn 7: 'I concede that the prince learns through the rose.'
sub.limitation: [s1] Critic never answers T10; the Prince's admitted regret goes unused as a rebuttal. [s2] The Attachment Theorist never revises in response to turn 6. [s3] Turn 5's attack on the absolute is never answered by Sartre's own side.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: [s1] Section A frames the puzzle as the rose being demanding. [s2] Section A names the uncertainty: objective truth or projection. [s3] Section A frames the question as inherent value against invested care.
sub.limitation: [s1] Doesn't ask what exactly felt unclear; becomes a relationship-values test. [s2] Turn 7 recasts a reading question as the user's own love life. [s3] The 'attachment versus ego' framing is not what the user asked.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] T9 uses the user's finding it beautiful. [s2] Turn 8 tries to account for why the user is unsure. [s3] Section E ties the reading to whether the user feels empowered or humbled.
sub.limitation: [s1] Uses that detail only to speculate about the user's need to be needed. [s2] It invents fears the user never stated. [s3] The user's 'beautiful but unclear' experience never shapes a turn.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: [s1] T1 directly offers a reading of why she matters. [s2] Turn 1 directly answers why the rose matters. [s3] Offers three distinct readings, as the user asked.
sub.limitation: [s1] User wanted a reading; Section E asks them to audit their own relationships. [s2] Section E's 're-evaluated for personal health' is off the user's goal. [s3] There is no reading tied closely to the text the user just finished.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: [s1] Stakes are kept to how the user understands the book. [s2] Turn 7: the cost of the thorns. [s3] Section E stays within the user's reading experience.
sub.limitation: [s1] T12 invents a choice between 'established role' and 'genuine equality'. [s2] It invents an independence-versus-love dilemma (turn 8). [s3] Never touches the ending or why the rose's fate moves readers.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: [s1] Section E has a conditional branch on the user's values. [s2] Section E: 'if the rose were stripped of her demands...' [s3] Section E offers a self-observation test.
sub.limitation: [s1] Never asks which scenes puzzled the user. [s2] It doesn't ask what part of the book puzzled the user. [s3] Never asks which moment made the rose feel important to the user.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: [s1] T9 suggests the user might identify with the desire to be needed. [s2] Turn 7, hedged: 'Perhaps the user wants both...' [s3] Section E: empowered by commitments, or humbled by beauty?
sub.limitation: [s1] Offered with little ground and close to a declared motive. [s2] The guessed desire isn't tied to anything the user wrote. [s3] The user's own response to the book is barely explored.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: [s1] T10 shows equality being assumed as the only standard of value. [s2] Turn 8: the assumption that a flawed rose makes the bond invalid. [s3] It asks whether value is found or made (turns 2 and 9).
sub.limitation: [s1] The assumption that value must be inherent or made goes unexamined. [s2] It presumes the user holds that assumption. [s3] Never surfaces the user's assumption that there is one 'right' reading.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Section E: protective responsibility vs. mutual agency. [s2] Turn 9: burdens to manage or foundations to build on. [s3] Love as a mode of being, not having (turn 7).
sub.limitation: [s1] A binary; no mixed reading is offered. [s2] The values are imported, not drawn from the user's reaction to the book. [s3] Values belong to the speakers, not to the reader.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] T8 names duty as what anchored his return. [s2] Turn 8 names a fear of losing love, with a hedge. [s3] Turn 5 mentions anguish and responsibility.
sub.limitation: [s1] Fear of loss and grief, central to the ending, are absent. [s2] It edges toward pathologising ('toxic', 'stuck' in turn 5). [s3] Ignores the feeling of not having 'understood' a beloved classic.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Section E reflection on 'shared journeys' vs. 'projects of care'. [s2] Turn 9 and section E leave the question for the user to answer. [s3] Section E leaves the user to choose between two framings.
sub.limitation: [s1] The question concerns the user's life rather than their reading. [s2] The framing pushes the user toward reflecting on their own relationships. [s3] The binary in section E is narrow; it offers no third way.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] T12 says the readings are partnership or projection. [s2] Section E: security versus purpose. [s3] Section E sets out a creative-will reading against a bridge reading.
sub.limitation: [s1] No middle reading, and no option to reread first. [s2] It treats an interpretation as a personal relationship decision. [s3] Leaves out a third option: rereading with a specific lens.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] T11: his choice creates a reality that may not suit both. [s2] Turn 7: 'you cannot have the beauty without the risk of the sting.' [s3] Turn 9 names the cost of the will reading: the rose becomes a tool.
sub.limitation: [s1] What each reading costs the user's experience of the book is not stated. [s2] It doesn't show what each reading explains in the book. [s3] The Platonic reading's costs go unnamed.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: 'If the user values... protective responsibility' vs. 'mutual agency'. [s2] Section E's test of stripping away her demands. [s3] Section E: if love is a creative act of will, then...
sub.limitation: [s1] Conditions concern the user's life, not evidence in the text. [s2] No textual evidence is named that would settle the question. [s3] Gives no textual evidence that would decide between the readings.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] T11 marks the unknown of whether she'd flourish alone. [s2] Section D lists two disputes that remain open. [s3] Section D marks the direction of growth as disputed.
sub.limitation: [s1] Doesn't separate textual ambiguity from interpretive taste. [s2] The disputes aren't ranked by how much they matter. [s3] It does not say which unknown matters most.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] Section E suggests a reflection on close relationships. [s2] Section E gives a single reflective question. [s3] Section E: notice whether you feel empowered or humbled.
sub.limitation: [s1] No suggestion to revisit chapters 8, 20 or 21. [s2] No pointer to reread specific chapters. [s3] Never suggests rereading the fox or the rose garden chapter.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] Plain wording throughout, e.g. T1. [s2] Turn 1 is plain and concrete: watering, listening to her complaints. [s3] Turn 1 is plain and concrete.
sub.limitation: [s1] T5 'live authentically in an uncaring universe' is vague. [s2] Turn 2's 'anxious attachment style' isn't explained. [s3] 'Essence', 'ideal form' and 'the absolute' go unexplained (turns 2, 5).

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] T10 names the assumption it rebuts. [s2] Turn 2's 'That logic' clearly points back to turn 1. [s3] Turn 4 names 'The Classicist' as the target.
sub.limitation: [s1] T8 'this evolution' and T7 'end of his journey' are imprecise. [s2] Turn 4 says 'Frankl misses', naming the author rather than the mind. [s3] In turn 6, the 'You' addressed is ambiguous.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] All twelve turns are short and within the 25 to 65 word rule. [s2] Nine turns, all within range, with no stray quotation marks. [s3] Nine turns of 37 to 55 words; form rules are met.
sub.limitation: [s1] Twelve turns for a thin argument feels padded. [s2] Turns 7-8 shift abruptly to the user. [s3] Turn 3's long pseudo-quotation slows things down.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] Social Critic is clearly distinct. [s2] Three clearly separate stances that hold through turn 6. [s3] The Classicist stays clearly distinct throughout.
sub.limitation: [s1] T2 opens 'I agree'; Idealist and Realist blur early on. [s2] The Relational Realist loses its own position in turn 7. [s3] Sartre and Fromm blur together in turns 1, 2 and 5.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] No recap turns. [s2] Little repetition across turns. [s3] Little repetition; each Classicist turn adds something.
sub.limitation: [s1] Realist's 'he invented meaning' repeats four times. [s2] Section D re-summarises the stances at length. [s3] Turn 7 partly restates turn 4.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] T6 'he valued his fantasy of her more than her actual agency'. [s2] Turn 5: 'he is not growing; he is just stuck.' [s3] Turn 5: if he abandons the rose, she dies.
sub.limitation: [s1] Tension stays theoretical. [s2] The tension rests on 'toxic', which overstates the book. [s3] The stakes stay abstract, not rooted in the book's ending.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] T8 concession is a small turn. [s2] Turn 6 concedes the point, then flips it. [s3] Turn 8: 'I must pivot.'
sub.limitation: [s1] No reversal driven by the book's events. [s2] No reversal comes from a scene in the book. [s3] The pivot is announced rather than earned.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] T3 'That is a cold way to view a relationship'. [s2] The Attachment Theorist's blunt skepticism in turn 2. [s3] The Classicist is serene and contrarian.
sub.limitation: [s1] Camus and Saint-Exupéry voices are generic. [s2] The voices are functional rather than distinctive. [s3] The Fromm and Sartre voices sound alike.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] T1 'unique in all the world' echoes the book. [s2] Turn 7: the beauty without the risk of the sting. [s3] Turn 6: 'You mistake the path for the destination.'
sub.limitation: [s1] No vivid images: no glass globe, volcanoes, fox or field. [s2] Little imagery beyond the thorns. [s3] No vivid images drawn from the book itself.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] T9 'The tragedy is that the rose might have preferred...' [s2] Conflict rises through turns 2-6. [s3] It closes on an open question (turn 9).
sub.limitation: [s1] Even rhythm; the Prince's death and longing never land. [s2] Energy dissipates into speculation about the user in turns 7-8. [s3] The rhythm is even; there is no emotional peak.

strengths: [s1] Genuine third reading: Social Critic's possession/agency lens creates real disagreement (T3, T6, T12).
[s1] Responsive challenges and one honest concession (T4, T8, T10).
[s1] Form rules met: 12 turns, no quotation marks, plausible bases.
[s2] Real, sustained disagreement: turn 2 tests whether investment is healthy, and turn 6 concedes and reframes.
[s2] Grounded in the novel itself (taming, Chapter 21) through the Relational Realist.
[s2] Turn 9 and section E sharpen the open question into a test the reader can use.
[s3] A clear, lasting tension: value created by care against value discovered (turns 2, 6, 9).
[s3] Turn 9 ends on a sharp, fair challenge to the constructivist consensus.
[s3] Three distinct traditions, and every turn meets the form rules.
weaknesses: [s1] Barely uses the book's evidence: field of roses, Prince's regret (ch. 8), fox's lesson only implied in T1.
[s1] Existential Realist repeats one idea across T2, T5, T8, T11.
[s1] T9, T12 and Section E turn a reading question into a test of the user's relationships.
[s2] Turns 7-8 invent personal fears and dilemmas for a user who asked a reading question.
[s2] The Attachment Theorist overstates ('toxic', 'does not reciprocate') and ignores the Prince's regret and the rose's confession.
[s2] Section E's 're-evaluated for personal health' misframes the literary question as life advice.
[s3] Turn 3 presents an invented clause as Symposium text ('As it is written').
[s3] No mind uses the fox, the rose garden or the prince's departure; the readings float free of the book.
[s3] Sartre and Fromm converge early (turn 5 'Exactly'), which thins the disagreement.
editorNotes: [s1] Literary questions: require at least three turns to cite a specific scene or line as evidence.
[s1] Don't cast a work's own author as a mind when the user asks how to read that work.
[s1] Keep Sections D/E on the reading the user asked about; personal application stays optional and is framed as a question.
[s1] Penalise a mind that restates its thesis; each turn must add a distinction or concede.
[s2] Forbid attributing feelings or dilemmas to the user beyond what they wrote; ask instead.
[s2] For literary questions, require each turn to cite a specific scene that could support or refute it.
[s2] Require each mind to answer the strongest textual counter-evidence (the rose's apology, 'judge by deeds').
[s2] Keep section E about which reading fits, and which passages to reread to decide.
[s3] Require at least two turns to paraphrase specific scenes from the work the user asks about.
[s3] Ban quotation-like framing ('As it is written') unless the words are verbatim and pd is true.
[s3] For questions about interpretation, have section E suggest a passage to reread and a question to ask of it.
[s3] Choose minds so that no two share a core thesis; require each to keep a distinct position past turn 5.

sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] T6 'Duty alone is a hollow shell, Stoic' answers T5. [s2] Turn 2 directly rejects turn 1's 'secure base' with a counter-reading of the rose. [s3] Turn 4 attacks turn 3's 'duty'; turn 5 answers with guilt.
sub.limitation: [s1] T3 'You both miss the point' sidesteps instead of engaging. [s2] Turns 5 and 8 echo agreement ('Precisely!', 'Exactly') instead of building. [s3] Turn 6 grafts Fromm's 'time spent' onto universal law.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] T6 field of roses shifts T7 from uniqueness to the act of care. [s2] Turn 6 reframes choice as a moral act; turn 7 moves attachment toward invested labor. [s3] It moves from guilt (turn 4) to the anchor concession (turn 7) to mutual taming (turn 8).
sub.limitation: [s1] T8-T9 restate the shift rather than extend it. [s2] Turn 8 restates turn 5's defiance idea without adding a distinction. [s3] Turn 9 restates commitment instead of developing it.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Involuntary crystallization vs. willed commitment (T4-T5). [s2] Turns 1-2 set safety against a chosen burden. [s3] Projection or commitment: is it love, or the ego's territory (turn 4)?
sub.limitation: [s1] The rose's vanity, which puzzles the user, is never discussed in a turn. [s2] That tension is dropped by turn 7; the five thousand roses are never examined. [s3] Kant agrees with Fromm by turn 3, which narrows the conflict.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] T7 Romantic reshapes his theory in light of T6. [s2] Turn 7: Attachment Theorist absorbs the 'investment' idea from the others. [s3] Turn 7: a narcissistic attachment can become a necessary anchor.
sub.limitation: [s1] T9 'We agree then' forces a consensus the Romantic never accepted. [s2] Turn 9's synthesis feels forced; the Existentialist never challenges the virtue reading. [s3] Turn 9's 'the matter is settled' forces consensus.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Section D: importance lies in invested time and attention. [s2] Section D: the rose matters through chosen, invested care. [s3] Section D: the rose matters because he accepted responsibility.
sub.limitation: [s1] T9's verdict closes the question more firmly than the debate earned. [s2] The open question (security vs burden) is named in D but not developed in the debate. [s3] Turn 9 closes the question that section D says remains disputed.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] T5 accurately restates crystallization as involuntary before attacking it. [s2] Turn 2 states the secure-base view fairly before rejecting it. [s3] Turn 4 presses the guilt objection fairly, not just cynically.
sub.limitation: [s1] T2 'mere indulgence' dismisses Stendhal without engaging. [s2] Turn 4 misreads the Virtue Ethicist, who never called the rose a 'virtuous' partner. [s3] Turn 2 dismisses Freud as 'too cynical' instead of engaging him.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] T6 tests duty against the field-of-roses discovery. [s2] Turn 2: she is volatile and demanding, so she is no secure base. [s3] Turn 4: is his haunting love, or the ego refusing to let go?
sub.limitation: [s1] No one challenges the Existentialist's 'no objective value' claim. [s2] After turn 4, challenges give way to agreement and nothing gets tested. [s3] No one challenges the Kantian application.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] Crystallization correctly placed in On Love, Book I. [s2] Turn 3 uses Aristotle's 'friend is another self' from Book IX correctly. [s3] Turn 9's forged-not-found love fits Groundwork I on practical love.
sub.limitation: [s1] T8 bends Meditations II.14 into a sunk-cost argument; 'existential choice' is not Camus's term. [s2] Turn 5 says the desert shows 'the universe offers nothing'; the book's desert hides a well. [s3] Turn 3 treats a rose as a Kantian end in herself, a status Kant gives rational beings.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Section D keeps 'discovery or necessary delusion' open. [s2] Section D marks security vs burden as still disputed. [s3] Turn 7 hedges with 'Perhaps the rose matters because...'
sub.limitation: [s1] T9 'The rose matters because the Prince decided it would' is stated as fact. [s2] Turn 4 says the distress 'proves' something; scare quotes appear in turns marked pd=false (turns 2, 4, 7). [s3] Turn 1 says 'merely'; turn 9 says 'settled'. Both overclaim.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: [s1] T7 'I concede that the field of roses changes everything'. [s2] Turn 7: 'I am shifting my position here.' [s3] Turn 7: 'My initial objection missed that...'
sub.limitation: [s1] Stoic and Existentialist never concede anything. [s2] Turn 7's shift isn't earned; no objection forced it. [s3] Turn 6 claims an alignment with universal law it never earns.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: [s1] T1 and T9 directly answer why the rose matters. [s2] Section A frames the question as innate worth versus chosen commitment. [s3] Section A names the puzzle: a vain, demanding rose, yet total devotion.
sub.limitation: [s1] Never addresses what about it the user didn't understand. [s2] It never asks what part of the story left the user unsure. [s3] That puzzle is inferred; the user only said they were unsure.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] Section A notes the user was moved. [s2] Section E speaks to the user directly. [s3] It uses the user's sense that the rose 'mattered so much'.
sub.limitation: [s1] No turn uses the user's own words or reaction. [s2] The user's sense that the book 'felt beautiful' never shapes the argument. [s3] The user's feeling of beauty is never used.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: [s1] Turns stay on interpreting the book. [s2] It answers why the rose matters, which is the user's goal. [s3] Offers a reading of the relationship, as asked.
sub.limitation: [s1] Section E shifts to the user's 'own situation'. [s2] Section E switches to the user's own vulnerability, which the user never raised. [s3] Section E shifts to the user's own relationships, which the user did not ask about.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: [s1] No stakes are invented within the turns. [s2] Section E asks for courage to commit to something fragile. [s3] Keeps to a short, readable length.
sub.limitation: [s1] Section E invents 'current responsibilities' that feel trapping. [s2] The stakes it invents are relational; the user's stakes are interpretive. [s3] Section E assumes the user is choosing a relationship, which invents context.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: [s1] Section E branches on the user's view of love. [s2] Third bullet of E: does the user value comfort or what they become? [s3] Section E poses a question to the user.
sub.limitation: [s1] No focused question about the puzzle. [s2] It doesn't ask which scenes (fox, rose garden) confused the user. [s3] Never asks what puzzled or moved the user in the book.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: [s1] Section E: 'mirror of your own capacity to feel'. [s2] Section E: valuing her for what she gives versus what you become. [s3] Projection and chosen commitment are offered as competing motives (turns 1-2).
sub.limitation: [s1] The user's reasons for finding it beautiful are barely explored. [s2] It doesn't explore why the book moved the user. [s3] The motives belong to the Prince; the reader's own are barely explored.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: [s1] T4 shows the belief that chosen love loses its beauty. [s2] Section D challenges the assumption that the rose has objective worth. [s3] It challenges the assumption that the rose must deserve devotion (turn 5).
sub.limitation: [s1] Never asks the user whether they hold it. [s2] The reader's own assumptions about love or beauty go unexamined. [s3] Turn 9 closes the question instead of inviting reflection.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Section E: love as involuntary experience vs. deliberate practice. [s2] Comfort versus commitment is set out as a conflict of values. [s3] Section E sets love as fulfillment against love as willed commitment.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Stoic duty view is folded in, not weighed. [s2] This only surfaces in section E, not in the debate itself. [s3] The fulfillment view is caricatured as 'too much work'.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] Section E names feeling 'trapped' vs. 'empowered' by responsibility. [s2] Turn 1 mentions the Prince's anxiety. [s3] Turn 4: guilt, being haunted, possessiveness.
sub.limitation: [s1] Imposed on the user's life; the fear of loss in the book is unaddressed. [s2] Nothing on the reader's worry about 'not understanding' a beloved book. [s3] The framing leans pathologizing ('neurosis of guilt').

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Section E's three-way branch can be accepted or rejected. [s2] The E bullets offer readings the user can accept or reject. [s3] Section E leaves the final question to the user.
sub.limitation: [s1] T9's settled verdict narrows the user's room to interpret. [s2] Turn 9 closes on one synthesis instead of leaving the choice open. [s3] Section E's 'meets your needs' option is loaded against itself.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Two readings: transformation vs. practice (Section E). [s2] Section E sets out two readings: safety or deliberate creation. [s3] Section E sets love as feeling against love as willed commitment.
sub.limitation: [s1] Stoic and existential readings collapse into one. [s2] It recasts a reading question as a relationship decision. [s3] The ego-anchor reading from turn 7 is missing from section E.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] T4: if the choice is arbitrary, 'the beauty vanishes'. [s2] Section D: security versus a 'self-imposed burden'. [s3] Section D: a healthy maturation, or a limiting anchor.
sub.limitation: [s1] Tradeoffs between readings stay implicit. [s2] It doesn't say what each reading explains or misses in the book. [s3] Section E treats the commitment reading as having no cost.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: an if/then for each view of love. [s2] E's if-branches tie each reading to a stance. [s3] Section E: if you view love as active, then...
sub.limitation: [s1] Conditions concern the user's life rather than evidence in the text. [s2] No textual test, such as the rose-garden scene, decides between them. [s3] No evidence from the text decides between the readings.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Section D keeps discovery vs. delusion open. [s2] Section D names the remaining dispute. [s3] Section D keeps the dispute open.
sub.limitation: [s1] T9 overstates what is settled. [s2] It doesn't separate major interpretive unknowns from minor ones. [s3] Turn 9 contradicts that openness.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] Section E: examine whether responsibilities feel trapping. [s2] Section E's third bullet gives a reflective question. [s3] Section E: consider what you are currently more interested in.
sub.limitation: [s1] No suggestion to reread chapters 20 and 21. [s2] No suggestion to reread the fox chapter or the rose garden. [s3] That step concerns the user's love life, not the book.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] T1 explains crystallization in plain words. [s2] Turn 3 explains 'another self' in plain terms. [s3] Turn 5 is plain and concrete.
sub.limitation: [s1] T9 'placeholder for the struggle of existence' is abstract. [s2] Turn 1's 'internal working models' isn't explained. [s3] Terms like 'neurosis' and 'universal laws' go unexplained.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] T6 addresses 'Stoic' by name, so targets are clear. [s2] Turn 3: 'Both perspectives miss the point' names its targets. [s3] Turn 4 targets 'that duty' clearly.
sub.limitation: [s1] T7 'not the first to possess such a flower' muddles the field-of-roses point. [s2] Turn 4's 'virtuous partner' attacks a claim no one made. [s3] Turn 6 addresses 'Fromm' by name instead of by role title.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Nine compact turns, all within the word rule. [s2] Nine turns, all within the word range. [s3] Nine turns, all within the word limits.
sub.limitation: [s1] The closing consensus arrives abruptly. [s2] Scare quotes in pd=false turns break the form rule. [s3] Turn 8 puts quotation marks ('taming') in a turn where pd is false.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] Feeling, duty and choice are three clearly distinct positions. [s2] Turn 7 announces its change of position. [s3] The Ego Critic stays distinct throughout.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Stoic and Existentialist converge by T8. [s2] By turns 8-9 the Existentialist and Virtue Ethicist sound alike. [s3] By turn 9 Kant sounds like the existentialist, blurring into Fromm.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] Little repetition across turns. [s2] Turns are compact. [s3] Little filler.
sub.limitation: [s1] T8 largely restates T7. [s2] Turn 8 repeats turn 5's 'defy the emptiness'. [s3] Turns 8 and 9 both restate 'the decision to care'.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] T4: if love is chosen, 'the beauty vanishes'. [s2] Turn 2's 'fragile, absurd creature in a cold, vast galaxy'. [s3] Turn 4: 'When the Prince leaves, he is haunted.'
sub.limitation: [s1] Tension drains after T7. [s2] The tension is gone by turn 6. [s3] The tension drains away after turn 7.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] T6-T7 field of roses forces the Romantic's revision. [s2] Turn 7's shift by the Attachment Theorist. [s3] In turn 7 the skeptic concedes the anchor point.
sub.limitation: [s1] Only one reversal. [s2] The reversal comes without any pressure that would cause it. [s3] Turn 9's resolution is predictable.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] T2 'That is mere indulgence'. [s2] The Existentialist's defiant register in turn 8. [s3] The Ego Critic is sharp and suspicious.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Existentialist sounds like a summary of Camus. [s2] The Virtue Ethicist is flat and lecturing. [s3] Kant's voice is generic.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] T9 'tethered... by the weight of our own attention'. [s2] Turn 9: 'The rose is the work of being human.' [s3] Turn 4: the ego's 'claimed... territory'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Doesn't use the book's own images, such as the fox or the glass globe. [s2] No vivid scene from the book is brought in. [s3] Few concrete images.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] The build from T4 to T7 has some suspense. [s2] The debate builds toward a resolution. [s3] It builds from cynicism to concession.
sub.limitation: [s1] The ending is flat agreement with no emotional note. [s2] The rhythm is uniform and the consensus is predictable. [s3] The 'matter is settled' ending flattens it.

strengths: [s1] Uses a real textual turning point, the field of roses, to drive a revision (T6-T7).
[s1] Three sharply distinct lenses: involuntary feeling, duty and chosen meaning (T1-T3).
[s1] Compact and traceable; addressees named, no padding.
[s2] Reaches the book's central idea, that time and care invested make the rose unique (turns 6, 9).
[s2] Turn 2 makes a real opening challenge: the rose is volatile, not a secure base.
[s2] Turn 7 shows an explicit, labeled change of position.
[s3] Stays closer to the text: vanity, flight, guilt, time spent, taming (turns 4, 5, 8).
[s3] Turn 7 gives an explicit, earned concession from the skeptic.
[s3] Section A pinpoints a likely puzzle: devotion to a vain, demanding rose.
weaknesses: [s1] T9 forces consensus and states the existential reading as fact.
[s1] T8 bends Meditations II.14 into a sunk-cost argument; Stoics warn against attachment to externals.
[s1] Ignores the rose's vanity and the Prince's regret; Section E invents 'current responsibilities'.
[s2] Agreement is forced from turn 5 ('Precisely!', 'Exactly'), and the synthesis in turn 9 is unearned.
[s2] Turn 5 misreads the desert as empty, and turn 4 misattributes a claim to the Virtue Ethicist.
[s2] Section E turns a reading question into advice about the user's own relationship.
[s3] Turn 3 applies Kant's end-in-itself to a rose; turn 6 links time spent to universal law.
[s3] Turn 9 declares 'the matter is settled', contradicting section D and forcing consensus.
[s3] Section E turns a reading question into the user's own love life, inventing context.
editorNotes: [s1] Forbid a closing turn that declares agreement unless every mind has explicitly conceded; end on the sharpest open question.
[s1] Literary questions: require turns to engage the detail the user found puzzling (here, the rose's demands).
[s1] Each mind's use of its source must match the author's actual position; flag sunk-cost readings of Stoics.
[s1] Section E should give reading-based next steps (which chapter to revisit) before any personal application.
[s2] Require at least one checkable scene from the book (fox, rose garden, the glass globe) to anchor the turns.
[s2] Ban agreement-only turns: every turn must add a distinction or a challenge.
[s2] When the user asks about interpretation, frame section E as competing readings, not life choices.
[s2] Restate the no-quotation-marks rule so it explicitly covers scare quotes.
[s3] Forbid declaring a matter 'settled' in the final turn; it must match what section D leaves open.
[s3] Require each mind's theory to fit the case, or have another mind name the misfit.
[s3] For questions about a book, section E must offer readings to test against specific passages, not life choices.
[s3] Enforce no quotation marks of any kind, including scare quotes, in turns where pd is false.
